Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, who is in Toronto looking for help-he did not find any, I do not believe, either-my question is to the Minister of Science and Technology who is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, because I do not think he realizes he is the Minister of Science and Technology.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MINTING OF GOLD BULLION COIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform the House, on my behalf and on behalf of the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras), of the government's decision to undertake a three-year program for the sale of gold bullion coins. This decision stems mainly if not exclusively from the request made to that effect by our Canadian gold mine operators. The gold mining industry, which is concentrated mainly in Ontario, Quebec and the Northwest Territories, employs 4,700 people. Canada, which is the third largest gold producer in the world, will thus be following in the footsteps of the two first producers, South Africa and the U.S.S.R., which are also selling gold bullion coins, and will be slightly ahead of the United States which will likely undertake a similar program next year.
To give an idea of the extent of this over a billion dollar program, at today's rate of exchange, need I only say that it will require, over the next three years, a total of five million

ounces of gold, equal to the amount of gold extracted from Canadian mines in the last three years. It is our hope that this program, a first in the history of the Royal Canadian Mint, will be an incentive to our industry, as it has been indicated to me. It is certainly my most heartfelt wish.
In other words, my dear colleagues, the government's sole interest in the sale of such gold bullion coins, is to help our gold mines. Accordingly, during this three-year trial period, the five million ounces of pure gold will be supplied exclusively by our Canadian gold mines or from government reserves. Also, to limit and even preclude any risk of deficit, the government has decided to give the Royal Canadian Mint total and exclusive responsibility over all aspects of this gold bullion coin program, both in Canada and abroad.

As the minister has said, this is a billion dollar market. When the Americans put gold bullion on the market, hundreds of thousands of bids were made, far surpassing the amount of gold which was made available. The program has turned out to be a hedge against oil price inflation and inflation in general. It is also a hedge against bankruptcies in the business world and against bank bankruptcies, which are a fact of life in various countries around the world. For that reason gold bullion coins which are backed by the Mint, sold by the Mint and handled by the Mint will assure buyers around the world that they are getting exactly what they are paying for. This will enable buyers to trade these coins without any question as to value.
Some resentment was felt by people buying Kruger rands because of South Africa's policy. The Canadian coin overcomes one difficulty in that we are making it a coin of the realm. Certainly the $50 face value has no relationship to the purchase price because to buy this coin at today's market price cost Canadians $300. So it is not what you call a face value coin; it is a coin of the realm. The Kruger rand is not.
From the 23 lode mines in Canada in 1977 only about 1,717,000 ounces of gold were produced. To produce this gold the employment of about 5,000 miners in those 23 gold mines was needed. These mines produce an export value for Canada of about $239 million. If Canada enters this field where we are producing only 1.7 million ounces of gold per year, production must increase if we are to meet the requirements; otherwise, any shortfall will have to be made up from the reserves in our treasury.
I hope, along with other members of the House, that the government will assist the gold mining industry to find a ready market, a market that is available to the small producers as well as the large ones who do not have a marketing agency of their own. In effect the government through the Mint is going

That, Mr. Speaker, is a very important and sensitive question. For the time being, I can tell the hon. member that it will be the responsibility of the board of directors of the Royal Mint. Since the government's decision has just been taken, the board of directors has not yet reached a final decision as to the course to be followed. However, according to my preliminary discussions with the president of the Royal Mint, it seems that the marketing methods used by South Africa, which, of course, is a much bigger producer than Canada, will be followed rather closely. South Africa issues some eight million gold coins every year. As for us, we will issue some two million.
Apparently, various aspects will have to be considered. Firstly, the dealer should already be in the gold business, he should be able not only to sell gold, but also to buy it back from investors wishing to sell it, and should meet other criteria which will be defined by the Royal Mint.
So, the various details pertaining to distribution have not yet been worked out by the Royal Canadian Mint whose responsibility it will be. What we know for sure is that huge amounts of money will be involved, over a billion dollars, and that profits will be almost non-existent for the Mint; in other words, on the one hand very little profit is expected, while on the other hand, the risk involved is pretty high. That is why the Royal Mint has agreed to implement this program provided it is given the sole responsibility for it, from A to Z. Let us not forget that the price of the coin will vary on a daily basis, depending on gold market prices. Already, in the two major nations involved in this field, the U.S.S.R. and South Africa, there is in operation a system of sales to the wholesalers, which

we cannot change, and which is based on the day to day price of gold plus three per cent.
Therefore, it is with that 3 per cent that the Royal Mint will have to defray all its costs and also the current price of gold plus 3 per cent charged to the wholesaler. So the Mint cannot afford to make any mistake, otherwise we would incur tremendous losses.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted the other day at six o'clock I was explaining that Canadians, by any standard, are among the best housed people in the world, and that this was not only conjecture, it was the fact. This fact has been confirmed recently, as I was explaining to the House, by a Gallup poll taken across Canada last October. It showed that more than 85 per cent of Canadians were satisfied with their housing. Even in the Atlantic region where economic problems are more severe, more than 78 per cent of the people indicated satisfaction with their housing. The question asked of Canadians at the time was: "Are you satisfied, dissatisfied, or have no opinion about your housing situation?"
It was very interesting to note that this satisfactory response was given consistently by people of all ages, of all economic groups and in all parts of the country. Without question, the majority of Canadians are satisfied with their housing.
It is particularly reassuring, as I was indicating in my earlier remarks, that the degree of satisfaction has grown during the course of the last ten years. When a similar Gallup poll was conducted ten years ago the degree of satisfaction was only around 60 per cent and it is now over 85 per cent. The degree of dissatisfaction expressed at that time was 34 per cent, and this has now declined to 13 per cent.

One of the main reasons why people are satisfied with their housing is that an ever increasing proportion of this production consists of good quality housing of relatively small size which middle income families can afford. With our Assisted Home

February 23, 1979
Housing
Ownership Program and our rental housing program, we have managed during the last few years to decrease the production of highly priced homes and to increase that of accommodation which meets the need of the average Canadian family. From the inception of those two programs, from 1973 to 1977, 240,000 good units have been built at reasonable prices. The success of those programs not only helped a quarter of a million families to get good housing but also helped stabilize the prices of new and older dwellings. In fact, in 1977, the price of new housing units increased by 3.3 per cent only while the personal available income increased by almost 9 per cent.
Not only did we produce a larger number of housing units, Mr. Speaker, but we also improved on the quality of these units. Whereas in the early 1950s, 52 per cent of homes did not have central heating or electricity, this percentage has now fallen to less than 10 per cent. The percentage of homes without running water, hot or cold, was 43 per cent of all existing homes 25 years ago and is now down to 4 per cent only. The situation keeps on improving rapidly. Meanwhile, through our rehabilitation program, we have spent some $225 million to repair more that 50,000 units located in urban and rural areas, in order that they meet acceptable sanitary and security standards and that their usefulness be extended for another 15 years.
All those policies have been launched, needless to say by officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Obviously these directives come from the management of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Before the House takes recess for one hour, I would like to draw the attention of the House and of Mr. Speaker to the presence in the gallery of the Speaker of the five members of the private sector who sit on the board of directors of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation: Mr. McGloan, a lawyer from Saint John, New Brunswick; Mr. Jacques Plante, a businessman from Quebec city; Mr. Conrad Pinette, a businessman from Williams Lake, British Columbia; and, a noticeable fact of which I am proud, two most competent ladies: Mrs. Christine McKee, an urbanist at the University of Winnipeg and Mrs. Sylvia Sutherland, a journalist and member of civil organizations in Peterborough, Ontario.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is my third contribution in this debate in support of the bill before this House. Obviously, our rules do not allow a member to speak three times at the same stages of a debate, but the public and the members of this House will understand that, on the two previous occasions, I have been interrupted by the adjournment of the House.
When we adjourned at lunch time, Mr. Speaker, I was referring to the many reasons why 85 per cent of Canadians are satisfied with housing policies in Canada. This morning, I explained with a series of figures, the reasons why they are satisfied and those figures show outstanding progress as concerns the building of housing units for low-wage earners and senior citizens who need adequate housing.
Mr. Speaker, the figures I quoted this morning are important because they give the exact picture of the housing situation in Canada. They clearly show, I think, that in most cases, Canadians are living in relatively high quality housing. I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that such a high quality was reached only through the efforts of the federal government. Obviously, private builders and private financial institutions have played an essential role, as did other government levels. Mr. Speaker, I will unhesitatingly say that it would have been impossible to reach such a high level of performance without the help of the National Housing Act and programs and policies administered by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which is an agency of the Canadian government responsible for housing and community planning.
More than half of Canadian householders own their houses. And out of this number, half do not have mortgage debts nor is it necessary that they have any as the Progressive Conservative proposal made by the Leader of the Opposition would have them in order to benefit from this reactionary mortgage tax credit.
Mr. Speaker, I do not claim that we should rest on our laurels and be complacent about the housing situation in Canada. Obviously there is room for improvement. But as we now meet the needs of most Canadians as far as housing is concerned it becomes increasingly urgent to direct our efforts and resources toward the minority of Canadians who cannot provide for their own needs and who do not find help in the existing programs.
In this regard, the recent Gallup poll asked Canadians whether they were satisfied with the present housing situation in Canada. It is very interesting to analyse the motives of the few who declared themselves dissatisfied. As I was saying previously, this poll taken at the end of 1978, showed that 85 per cent of the people were satisfied and only 13 per cent were dissatisfied with the housing situation in Canada.
February 23, 1979

A breakdown of this 13 per cent of dissatisfied people shows that the major problem is high cost and-
I have some statistics that I would like to give to hon. members. Out of the 13 per cent who declared they were dissatisfied with housing, 17 per cent said their living accommodation was too small, that there was not enough space, that the kitchens were too small and there were not enough bedrooms; 8 per cent who were living in rental accommodation said they would prefer to live in houses of their own; a big chunk of the dissatisfied, representing 33 per cent of the 13 per cent of Canadians not satisfied with their housing, said that their housing was too expensive or hard to heat; 9 per cent complained of rundown accommodation, the need for repairs, inadequate plumbing and so forth, and 10 per cent said they felt they were living in an unsuitable neighbourhood. All this dissatisfaction must be looked into.
We are not without housing problems, Mr. Speaker. It is certainly clear that many Canadians are not well housed. It is an urgent concern of the federal government that our efforts and resources be directed to improving living conditions for those people who cannot provide for themselves.
Federal housing policies and programs have always been developed in response to the need that prevails at any given time. As market and economic conditions change, as the wants, needs and even the tastes of the Canadian people change, so does the federal approach to housing. In order to respond realistically to change CMHC must continue to fill a useful and effective role as a national housing agency.
We know that in metropolitan Canada about 155,000 households have inadequate or unsuitable dwellings and cannot afford better accommodation without spending over 30 per cent of their income to obtain it. Of these households only about 73,000 live in dwellings that could be improved; the rest would have to move in order to have adequate shelter.
In addition, about 283,000 households pay more than 30 per cent of their income for suitable and adequate shelter. Most of these people live in the older, central areas of cities and towns. In many cases these areas extend outward from the city core along railway tracks, are near airports or are mixed with or adjacent to industrial areas. In these central neighbourhoods housing stock is usually of poor quality while the level of community services is consistently inadequate. These problems are well known and obviously they are known to the opposition.

When we made this report public, showing that there are over 150,000 families living in unsatisfactory housing in Canada, the Progressive Conservative critic on housing cried shame. Here is what Professor Lawrence Smith said in an interview over the CTV network on Canada AM about the indignation of the Progressive Conservative critic on housing
Housing
matters. Professor Smith was interviewed by the commentator Norm Perry.

Part of Mr. Perry's interview with Lawrence Smith, who is a professor at Toronto University, went as follows:
-Jean Pigott, the Conservative MP, she made public a report by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and she quotes from that report and she says, "Look, according to this report, CMHC says 150,000 households in this country are in inadequate housing." Now, that sounds pretty frightening. Is she right?
Smith: -well, I would look at it just the opposite. I can't say that the number is wrong, but I wouldn't think that's frightening at all. I would think that that's a great endorsement of the housing policy and the housing industry. Because there's about 7% million households in Canada, so what that says is that there's two per cent, or just under two per cent of the households that are in inadequate housing, and that's a phenomena] compliment to policy-makers over the years and the housing industry.
Perry: -So that's really a taking out of context thing, then, isn't it? In other words, when you say 150,000 inadequate housing it sounds bad. You say it's only two per cent of the houses in this country, and it's pretty good.
Smith: -That's right. It's about, oh, six or eight months' construction.
Perry: -Okay. She also claims (and again she's quoting from CMHC) 438,000 households are spending more than 30 per cent of their income on housing, which suggests that houses are very expensive. Now, I don't think that's any surprise to anybody, but for 438,000 people to be spending more than 30 per cent of their income on housing, that sounds pretty scary.
Professor Smith replied:
Well, once again, you have to put all this in context. That comes out to only six per cent of the total households in the country, which then isn't a staggering amount. Second of all, you have to look at who it is that's spending this. For example, if a young family buys-stretches and buys a house and they end up spending 30 or 35 per cent of their income in the First year or two because they expect their incomes are going to rise, and Five or 10 years later it will be down to 25 or 22 per cent, that's not scary at all. On the other hand, if it happens to be elderly or people on Fixed incomes, where they have no hope of rising incomes and maybe will face rising housing costs, then there's a hardship problem for them.
But, again, the interpretation of this shouldn't be that there's problems in the housing industry. The interpretation of too high a proportion of income going to housing could well be that there are some families and households that have too low an income.

Mr. Speaker, there is a summary of what Professor Smith said in this television interview while commenting on the criticism passed by the Progressive Conservative opposition on housing in Canada. That is what I would have said myself. It is obvious, when one considers the whole housing situation in Canada, putting it back in its true perspective, that not only housing production at an acceptable level and at an acceptable cost must be taken into account, but also the financial capacity of those who live in those homes.
There is no housing crisis in Canada. There may have been at the beginning of this decade, in the early seventies, ten years ago, a hint of crisis, but the Trudeau government did a remarkable job during the last ten years to remedy this problem and solve in an outstanding way the deficiencies and difficulties which existed in the early seventies. Assuredly, the

February 23, 1979
Housing
job is not finished. There are certainly adjustments to be made. There are certainly improvements to be made yet.
And precisely, Mr. Speaker, this bill that we are considering today deals with such matters in amending the National Housing Act, first, to increase the building of public housing by non-profit organizations, second, to encourage much larger investments by the private sector in the housing area, third, to extend to all of Canada the Housing Rehabilitation Assistance Program.
Fourth, to set up an efficient housing program for our people. Five, to encourage and support co-operative housing in Canada. Six, to offer the borrower with lesser means another option through mortgage with graduated payments. And seven, to provide a community services program that will help the provinces and the municipalities give better service to their people. Those, Mr. Speaker, are seven actual measures to be found in this bill and which are designed to help those who are poorly housed, and those who are most in need of assistance, namely our low-income workers and our older citizens.
Naturally, those measures provide for the construction of a larger number of housing units for the needy. But, on the other hand, there are also those who are paying too much for their housing. But in their case, and I say it again, theirs is not so much a problem of housing as one of income. For them, as hon. members know, I announced earlier this week, in a speech I made in Toronto, that there was another solution to their problem, which strikes me as infinitely more just than that proposed by the loyal opposition in this House.
Now, Mr. Speaker, commenting on this bill gives me an opportunity to draw a parallel between the approach taken by the Progressive Conservative party and that taken by the Liberal party of Canada as regards the housing issue. There are obviously many differences between us and the Progressive Conservative party. Once again, when it comes to solving the housing problem in Canada we can see that the Progressive Conservative party is the party of the rich and well off while the Liberal party is the one which cares about the average citizen and the working class in Canada.

speechtext:
To return to the bill, I was discussing and explaining the fundamental difference in approach between the Conservatives and the Liberals. I was saying that the Conservative scheme would be much too expensive, a waste of good taxpayers' money. While the present government has adopted a firm policy of restraint in government expenditures, this does not mean that it has closed off the possibilities of initiatives to serve employment purposes in an efficient way and which offer relief to people who are in difficult economic circumstances.
Our primary objection to the idea of deductibility is that it is wasteful and inefficient as an employment generator. Above all, it is unfair and regressive in its income distribution effects. To generate employment through the housing market, it is necessary only to stimulate the construction or repair of housing. Funds expended for these purposes put people to work. It is not necessary or efficient from an employment point of view to attach subsidies to the entire occupied housing starts at enormous expense.
On the other hand, if the purpose of deductibility is simply to offer relief to people who cannot afford to occupy housing, then there is no reason to exclude the entire tenant population and no reason to accord aid to home owners in a deliberately perverse manner which tends to increase the aid with the level of income of the beneficiary household.
Let me elaborate quickly on this. I just mentioned that if deductibility had been in effect in 1976, it would have cost $2.1 billion. Of this amount tenants, who constitute 38 per cent of households and who have lower income on average than home owners, will get nothing. Households making less than $5,000 income, who constituted 21 per cent of all households in 1976, would also get nothing. Those earning from $5,000 to $15,000, who made up almost half the population in 1976, would get just over one-third of the benefits. The remaining 31 per cent of households, those earning over $15,000, would receive two-thirds of the entire benefits.

speechtext:
Indeed a Tory program. It clearly differentiates the approach to housing of Liberals and Conservatives.
A further point has to do with the interprovincial impact on deductibility which tends to favour provinces which have high income and high home owner propensity. The evidence is that on mortgage interest deductibility, only Ontario and British Columbia will gain relatively in the sense that the benefit to their citizens would be higher than their relative share of the number of households. All of the other provinces will benefit less than their share.
Housing
It is very interesting to see that the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada, HUDAC, decided that they cannot endorse the proposals of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) unless certain conditions are included, conditions that obviously cannot be met. A Canadian Press report of February 20, 1979, stated:
HUDAC said the resultant loss of tax revenue would have to be matched by cuts in government expenditures so that the government deficit would not be adversely affected as a result of the program.
It is impossible for the Conservatives to meet that point. Their scheme will only add substantially to the deficit of the Canadian government.
It also wanted assurance that the supply and price of mortgage money would not be adversely affected and that the "cyclical instability of the industry would not be aggravated".
Indeed, the builders of Canada have every reason to be frightened by these tremendous effects on the cyclical instability of the industry that would be hurt by such measures.
It is also interesting to look at the report of a member of parliament who went to the United States along with other members of this House to study their system. The purpose of the discussions was to assess the merits of their fiscal system which permits the deductibillity of mortgage interest and real estate taxes in computing incomes. The hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston) had this to report on his return to Canada:
The deductibility feature certainly favours upper income earners, not only because of the progressive nature of the rate structure in the United States but also because home owners in 1976 had an average of $16,000 while renters had an average income of $7,400.
The average price per home in the United States at the present time is approximately $61,000 and 63 per cent of U.S. housing is owner-occupied with a high of 69 per cent in some areas to a low in New York State of 47 per cent. It is important to note that in Canada in 1976, 63 per cent of all households were owned, which is identical with the U.S. experience and yet no mortgage interest or real estate taxes are deductible in this country.
So without such a beautiful scheme, our performance in Canada is very good, and we do not need regressive measures to complicate the situation.
The third matter reported by the hon. member for West-mount is the following:
The recommendation of all government officials and all independent economists with whom we met was to the effect that a system of mortgage interest and real estate tax deductibility is to be avoided at all costs... The problem which they all recognized is that once incorporated in a fiscal system, the deduction is impossible to eliminate.
Then it creates all kinds of embarrassment. I have explained the so-called miracle solutions to housing problems offered by the official opposition. On the other hand, the Liberal government has come forward with the series of measures included in this bill to tackle head on some of our main housing problems.
Our approach has been discussed with and approved by the provinces. Our solutions are eagerly anticipated by municipalities, co-operative movements and various non-profit organizations in Canada. What we want to do is economically sound, fiscally responsible, relevant and 100 per cent socially just. I

February 23, 1979
Housing
do not pretend that this bill will solve all problems, but there is no doubt that it will go a long way toward doing that.
I admit that the government will soon have to be concerned about the still large number of families which live in inadequate and unsuitable housing because they cannot afford satisfactory accommodation. We will have to consider the possibility of a more general kind of aid for people who have difficulty obtaining decent accommodation. This type of aid might be in the nature of shelter allowances. I recognize that this will require a very substantial commitment of government funds, and in a period of restraint such a scheme can hardly be implemented; but the reason I am talking about such a scheme today-while I recognize that funds are not presently available-is that I want to warn Canadians that there is a better way of solving housing problems in Canada than by adopting the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition, which would be detrimental.
There is no doubt that there is a better way of solving housing problems when money is available. It seems to me that the right direction has been taken by the governments of British Columbia and New Brunswick in the introduction of their shelter allowance programs for the elderly. Those programs assist the elderly with their rental payments, to the extent that those payments exceed 25 per cent of their incomes, and it is thus possible for those people to solve their housing problems better by choosing freely in the marketplace. I sincerely hope that in the near future and as soon as our economy permits we will adopt shelter allowance systems which will provide assistance to home owners and tenants alike through payment of tax credits for shelter expenditures exceeding a certain percentage of income.
Until then, the bill now under consideration will authorize the implementation of a new non-profit housing program which has been designed to increase the housing stock for low-income Canadians and eliminate many of the disadvantages of traditional federal-provincial housing programs.
I would like to take a few more minutes to outline this program, Mr. Speaker. First of all, it will operate through non-profit organizations, whether private church organizations, philanthropic clubs, unions or other similar organizations, or public organizations set up by municipal or provincial authorities.
These organizations, when they wish to build or buy low-cost rental housing, will be privately financed by banks, trust companies or credit unions recognized under the National Housing Act. To ensure that the organizations will be able to obtain easily such mortgage loans, the federal government will provide mortgage insurance under the provisions of the National Housing Act. This insurance will cover the whole value of these properties, not only in the case of the units to be built,
[Mr. Ouellet.)
but also in the case of existing housing to be purchased and repaired.
Everyone will be allowed to reside in these dwellings. Those with higher income will pay the rental rate necessary to make the project profitable. Those who cannot afford to pay the whole amount will pay a rent proportional to their income. Since many tenants will pay a lower rent than the viable economic rent, the residential projects will operate at a loss. These operational losses will be covered by a new system of federal grants which will provide a significantly higher contribution than the one previously provided through public housing programs.
I would now like to give a brief explanation of the mathematical methods used to set the amount of federal grants and rental rates. Firstly, under federal-provincial public housing programs, it is the provincial governments which set the rentals and administer the rental projects. This is not the responsibility of the federal government which has never set rentals and has no intention of doing so, either within the existing public housing programs or under the new non-profit housing program. Earlier this year and also at the end of 1978, it was falsely suggested that the federal government was gearing to increase rentals for tenants of public housing projects, which created some concern over the disastrous effect that such increases would have on low income families. As I said, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government does not set rentals and has no intention whatsoever to do so either in the public housing or in any other sector. Indeed, we could not increase or lower these rentals even if we wanted to, because we do not have the authority to do so, since this authority belongs primarily to municipal and provincial governments.
It is the provinces which set rentals, usually according to income-based scale. This scale varies greatly between provinces. In some, tenants pay a flat rate of 25 or 30 per cent, in others, the provincial government sets the percentage of income paid in rent. Also, the method of calculating household incomes and child benefits differs, as well as additional heating, electricity and parking costs.
Ever since 1970, the federal government has put out as guidelines for the provinces, rent scales which are based on what is considered as family income. Some provinces have made use of some of these guidelines, but not a single one of them is using them to their full potential. The rents thus proposed for housing units fully serviced, vary on the federal scale from 16.7 per cent in the case of the very low income people to 25 per cent for those with a slightly better income.
Hon. members are certainly aware of the fact that under the traditional programs of social housing, the federal government makes up jointly with the provinces for the operation deficits incurred when housing low-income people who are unable to pay commercial rates. The rent scales vary considerably from one province to the next, and so do the operation deficits. Therefore, the provinces which require their tenants to pay a
February 23, 1979

smaller share of their income for rent, run up deficits which are generally greater than those which require them to pay higher rents.
In order to treat all provinces equally, the Canadian government routinely pays, as a form of grant, any amount, however small, shown either on the provincial rent scale or on the proposed federal scale. As this scale has not been adjusted since 1970, whereas incomes, even that of the most underprivileged, have increased considerably since then, a very high proportion of tenants are receiving allocations based on 25 per cent of their income.
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians spend at least that much of their income for housing and some, especially the low-income earners who provide for their own needs without the benefit of public housing programs, spend a much greater share of their income on housing. While discussing the content of the new non-profit housing program with my colleagues, the provincial housing ministers, last year, I pointed out that there would be some advantages if they could all agree to phase over a period of time a uniform rent scale across Canada based, for instance, on a fixed rate of 25 per cent of gross income.
The provinces undertook to look into the matter and have in fact met several times in the past months to discuss this. From what transpired from their last meeting, I understand that they were unable to agree on the matter and a general consensus is therefore out of the question. This will have a very simple consequence: existing provisions will continue to be applied and each province will continue to use the scale it deems appropriate. As in the past, the federal government will pay the lesser of either the grant based on its proposed scale for public housing or the grant based on the current provincial scale. In any case, the grants should never exceed the actual operating deficit.
As provided by the new non-profit housing program, the total federal subsidy, for a particular project, will be sufficient to bring the interest rate down to 2 per cent. It will be the responsibility of the particular province to pay the other required subsidies. If a province pays a contribution which is equal to that of the federal government, the subsequent subsidies will be paid on a 50-50 basis by both governments.
The formula proposed by the Government of Canada is no doubt quite significant and very interesting, Mr. Speaker. One of the major problems faced by a non-profit organization interested in building and operating public housing units, is the interest rate it will have to pay over the years on the capital borrowed for such a project. So the decision of the Government of Canada to use its subsidy to bring down the prevailing interest rate to a fixed rate of 2 per cent is a considerable progress. It could substantially assist non-profitable organization in building and developing a greater number of housing projects.
There is no doubt that it will help if we say to those non-profitable organizations: Do not worry about the high rate
Housing
of interest you have to pay and which may go up over the years; no matter what it is, whether it be 8 per cent, 9 per cent, 10 per cent, 11 per cent, 12 per cent or even 14 per cent, I guarantee that for the duration of the project, until such time as you have reimbursed the capital, there is no doubt that we will grant you an annual subsidy to reduce that rate of interest, which may be 10 or 9 per cent, as I said, to 2 per cent. The difference between that 2 per cent and the 10 per cent or 11 per cent the market may be asking, you will receive each year in federal government grants.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this proposal will be of considerable help, not only to the non-profitable organizations in the private sector, but also, and especially, to those in the provincial and municipal sectors. To my mind, this program is equitable from the point of view of the tenants of housing sponsored by non-profitable organizations as well as from that of both federal and provincial governments. It respects in every point the stand I have taken during consultations with the provinces and the long-term policy of the Canadian government with regard to cost-sharing housing programs set up through joint federal and provincial initiative.
All the obstacles to the integral implementation of such a program have, to my mind, been removed, and I am optimistic about the achievement of its ultimate goal, namely, the annual construction of 30,000 good housing units for those in greatest need. I could add, Mr. Speaker, that one of the main instruments in getting this new housing program under way will be the housing co-operatives that played such an important role in the last few years in giving many Canadians access to decent housing which they could not have had without their help. From the start, we were concerned about seeing to it that those co-operatives would have every opportunity to participate fully in the program, and that nothing in the administration of the program would run counter to the principles on which the co-operative movement is based.
I am pleased to announce, Mr. Speaker, that following very extensive discussions with the Canadian Co-operative Housing Foundation we have reached an agreement which will help us achieve our respective objectives concerning the administration of grants and the Financial burden of the occupants. In addition to helping these housing co-operatives, we also want to open a new avenue to make housing available to low income individuals, and that is the rationale for another important principle contained in the bill. Indeed these amendments to the act will support and give more strength to our policy of relying as much as possible on private investment for housing construction and saving public funds for the kind of help only the government is able to offer.
Obviously, neither the federal government nor provincial governments have the resources required to meet all the needs in the area of housing in Canada. We believe the private sector

February 23, 1979
Housing
has financial resources that we must utilize in a more useful way, precisely to channel private funds into the implementation of the housing program.
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues are no doubt aware that mortgage insurance under the NHA is the major tool to stimulate private investment in housing, protecting as it does the lender against losses. The legislation put forward extends the provisions of the mortgage insurance program in a number of important ways to promote private sector investments and reduce government expenditures, which indeed is in line with our policy of reducing the Canadian government deficit.
The legislation would amend mortgage insurance provisions under the National Housing Act to make graduated payment mortgages more popular in private sector lending circles. Such a loan technique is a normal development of house ownership and rental housing programs. It would enable borrowers to reduce their monthly payments during the first year of occupancy, with later stabilization in the remaining payment period. Although this type of loan might not be the universal solution to housing problems, where put to proper use by lenders and borrowers it could indeed be most useful, particularly in the case of young people who start in life with limited revenues, as most people in similar circumstances, but who have every reason to believe their financial resources will increase as they advance in life.
I am pleased to indicate this new mortgage tool is finding increasing acceptance among both borrowers and financial people. As stated in the latest CMHC report, the corporation had insured graduated payment mortgages covering some 5,000 units. The legislation further provides that where a borrower defaults on his payments under an insured graduated payment mortgage, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will retake the loan and proceed with quick settlement with the lender.
Of course the Tory housing critic feels our experience in house ownership programs met with difficulties. She referred to defaults and foreclosures.
Some members opposite have asked me in the House about the percentage of defaults. They underlined the fact that according to them, about 10 per cent of those who took advantage of the Assisted Home Owership Program had defaulted. They remind me, Mr. Speaker, of that individual who complaints that his glass is 10 per cent empty when he should rejoice that it is still 90 per cent full.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of Canada took some risks with its Assisted Home Ownership Program when it encouraged certain people whose income were rather low and whose chances of becoming home owners were perhaps somewhat remote. Of course the Government of Canada took some risks, just as it is prepared to do when it offers the graduated payment mortgage and states that in case of default it will assume the debt and proceed quickly to settle with the lender. But we are prepared to take some risks,

because unlike the Conservatives who want policies for the benefit of the rich, we are prepared to implement policies which could endanger in some way the financial security of those transactions. We are prepared to take some risks for the benefit of middle income and even low-income people to allow them to take advantage, like any other Canadians, of the privilege and the opportunity to own their own house.
I do not hesitate to say that whatever criticisms the Progressive Conservative opposition may make on that issue and whatever percentage is involved, be it 2 per cent, 4 per cent, 5 per cent, or even 10 per cent, I prefer to let them play with those percentages concerning defaults and arrears. I am satisfied that we brought forward an outstanding program. Even though 10 per cent of those who benefited from those programs have failed to meet their payments, there are still another 90 per cent who did. We can be proud of that, because without this program 90 per cent of Canadians would not be home owners at present. We did not pass that motion.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I think that this bill will allow us, if it is adopted, to increase considerably the federal assistance to low-income people for the improvement of their housing. I heard the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) say that this assistance program to promote the purchase of houses was badly administered. By whom? Badly administered by that poor young couple who, some years ago, borrowed money in the hope of owning their house but who, for personal reasons, are no longer able to meet their payments, because they did not get the wage increase they expected to get, or because there was sickness in the family, or for any other personal reasons which prevented them from meeting their commitments. This has nothing to do with the Canadian government.
We said that we developed a program to promote home ownership and entered into an agreement with banking institutions so that they make funds available to Canadian borrowers while the Government of Canada granted subsidies to reduce the borrowing costs for new owners. If, unfortunately, some people could not take full advantage of the program, it is not our fault since we did not manage the program as the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) is suggesting.
We did not manage the program, we are only granting subsidies to reduce the cost for new owners. All we do is guarantee the loan made by the bank which normally, if we had not agreed to guarantee that loan, would not likely have loaned money to small or medium-income people. I think this attitude of the Progressive Conservative party which attacks such a fair and socially generous measure for small-income people to help them own their home shows clearly the true nature of that party in that they would never take a financial chance to help small-income people in Canada.
February 23, 1979

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us will, of course, contribute to increase the number of housing units. It is one of the prime objectives of the government. Furthermore, we want also, through this bill, to facilitate the restoration of Canadian residences. How many Canadians are living in an older house, that is not as comfortable and adequate as it was 10, 15, 20 or 30 years ago. But how many Canadians want to stay on living in that house because their father or grandfather lived in it, because it is located in a small town or a district where they know many people, where they feel at home!
Under its Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, the government has already spent millions of dollars to promote the rehabilitation of those residences. And we want to expand that program, because we believe that there is in Canada a large number of residences that are worth repairing and might be used for another 15, 20 or 30 years. It will be a cheaper way and probably a more humane way to answer the needs of those Canadian families who do not want a new house and choose to fill some holes or some cracks in the doors, the windows or the frame of their old house, who want to instal a new heating system and modernize their beautiful old house to make it more comfortable. And this bill, Mr. Speaker, specifically provides for a series of measures that will prompt the private sector to invest more in residential rehabilitation in Canada.
This bill will enable us not only to reach our goals in the housing field but also to obtain an even wider objective. It will enable the government to co-operate with other government levels so that all Canadians may live in a safe and pleasant environment. The community services program referred to in this bill is designed to carry out the second part of that commitment made by the Government of Canada which is to provide not only a good home for all Canadians, but also to give them a pleasant and secure environment. The federal aid to attain that objective will be provided so as to respect fully the levies made by municipal and provincial authorities to meet their needs and priorities and will remove most of the waste due to duplication of administrative procedures.
The community services program was discussed with the provincial minister concerned. It merges the federal assistance provided until now for neighbourhood improvements, water supply and sewage treatment facilities and for the construction of low rental and medium density housing. The federal government will continue, of course, to provide help in the form of direct grants for all those activities but it will extend from now on its assistance to a whole list of social, cultural and recreational services.
If I suggested extending the scope of the community services program it is because I realized that previous programs did not fully meet the needs of all Canadian municipalities and they needed precisely the flexibility required to allow them to have, if they so want, community and recreation centres, parks, ice rinks, child care centers, libraries, to allow them to improve
Housing
their municipal buildings as a municipal investment and to build plants for conversion of garbage into energy power and carry out all capital works considered priorities by those municipalities.
The new program, Mr. Speaker, is in line with the concept of block financing that was agreed upon by the provincial ministers at our meeting in Edmonton in February. The program provides that the federal government funds will be used for cummunity services in accordance with the purpose of the program but they will be distributed according to provincial and municipal priorities. I want to say that the various projects will not have to be approved by the Government of Canada, as was the case previously for the neighbourhood improvement program or the municipal infrastructure program. We are withdrawing all public servants in charge of the implementation, the monitoring or the administration of those programs. Finally, we are taking out one level of government in the use of those programs. We believe it is not necessary to have three levels of government represented in the management and administration of those programs. We trust municipal and provincial authorities to take care of that program by themselves. And, of course, we believe this program will meet the true priorities of Canadian municipalities much more adequately.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that in general this legislation is one of the important aspects of the Canadian government's position on housing in Canada. We can indeed be proud of our past accomplishments, but we want a better future still, because we are aware that there remain housing problems in Canada and that Canadian municipalities have major priorities which must be met. It is in this spirit of co-operation with provincial and municipal authorities as well as with public or private social housing agencies that the Canadian government wants to have a part in improving the production of Canadian homes, in a better environment, in all areas of our country.
I am not suggesting that this bill meets all the needs. As I have said, there is still progress to be made, and we will be able, in time, to meet other objectives, given the proper financial resources and to the extent, of course, of our financial capability.
Also, amendments to this bill may yet have to be brought in.
I do not pretend that we have solved everything. I have already received a few recommendations for amending certain minor aspects of the act, particularly with respect to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program where private financing should be made easier to obtain in order to get better results from that program.
1 know that the opposition parties will probably make proposals and introduce amendments to improve this bill. As for me, Mr. Speaker, and I say it now, any useful, constructive and worth-while proposal will be welcome and I am anxious to sit on that committee to deal with this bill clause by clause in

February 23, 1979
Housing
order to analyse it even further and if necessary to amend it in the best interest of all Canadians.
To conclude, I wish to say that it is the result of lengthy discussions with the provincial authorities. I know that they approve of this bill and 1 urge hon. members to do the same.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House are pleased to participate in second reading of this bill which embodies legislation to amend various sections of the National Housing Act. It is with great relief that I can finally rise in my place today on behalf of the thousands of municipalities in the provinces and the various third-sector groups who waited, some impatiently, for almost a year for this legislation to be debated and passed in this House. The minister has announced the various new programs four, five or six times-I have lost count.
Following release of the minister's new directions on housing last year, his attention, it would appear, has been on every direction except housing. He has either been preoccupied with planning an election that his leader is afraid to call or, as he
(Mr. Ouellet.]
stated this week in Toronto, he would prefer the value of the Canadian dollar to rise before doing anything except philosophize on housing problems. That includes the plight of 800,000 families who pay more than 25 per cent of their income for shelter. Everyone knows that if we waited for the Canadian dollar to rise under this government, our urban problems would multiply. A high priced dollar would make our exports more expensive, besides. Presumably his deputy minister would then have to peddle his grass huts internationally.
As I indicated earlier, it is almost a year since the minister announced his new direction. The government has deliberately contrived to schedule second reading of this bill at a time when municipalities are planning for funding following the termination of the old NIP program, and the non-profit and co-operative sectors have programs and prospects which have been unnecessarily delayed by this government's attempt to orchestrate quick passage of this bill without adequate examination and debate. But then again, careful examination and prudent lending are something that can be ignored particularly when luxury hotels are being financed with NHA money, or when the ministry directed CMHC to work on a system of patronage. The question is not so much the evolution of the policy of the lender of last resort but is a question of CMHC financing which resort. Mr. Speaker, we are not misled by this orchestration of a short time span on this bill. The minister has given a verbal commitment to the provinces that this legislation will be retroactive. He does not need to have quick passage and we intend to take as long as we can to debate this bill.
I should like to assure the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) that our unqualified support could be extended, but now I cannot.
The House and the people of this nation should have an opportunity to review the history of the ministry. The minister took quite a few diversions in the last hour so I shall spend a little time on the Ministry of Urban Affairs. I believe what has happened to the ministry symbolizes the failure of this government to assume its catalytic role in the determination of a national urban strategy. From its proclamation in this parliament in June, 1971, its mandate has been unfilled.
This government, lacking in any real commitment or sustained responsibility in the urban environment, has finally played this ministry as a card in the constitutional shuffle. The minister was never more accurate than when he stated before an audience Monday that "federal housing policies and programs have always been developed in response to the needs that prevailed at any given time." What resulted from these changing responses, to any given time on which the urgent drove out the important, was considerable confusion as to what assistance was available, what assistance had been withdrawn, and what the implementation dates were that were constantly being revised.
I wonder, sometimes, whether the minister has ever gone to see the mess he has created in some of the regions of the country. In more cases than not, "urgent" meant "elections" or "empire reorganization". There was never any continuity and stability in program operation. This prompted one provin-
February 23, 1979

cial official to state that Ottawa should get out of the numbers game and commit themselves to supporting longer-term principles and goals. He commented that the numbers can change or be reviewed every year, but the principles should remain.
The ministry was established to co-ordinate between federal agencies. It was to initiate policy proposal and evaluate both established federal policies affecting urban Canada, and proposals for change. It was to foster co-operative relationship in respect of urban affairs with the provinces and, through them, their municipalities, and with the public and private organizations. Certainly not least, it was to initiate, conduct, co-ordinate and recommend research related to urbanization.
It is interesting to note what transpired. In 1973 the government directed that a senior interdepartmental committee on urban affairs be established at the deputy minister level to co-ordinate government involvement in urban affairs. That committee, from all accounts, never met.
The policy research function of the ministry which is central to its mandate, hardly exists, if it exists at all. This led one former director general of the ministry to state publicly:
There is an irresistible presumption in the events of the past eight years that Trudeau rationalism, in so far as the urban policy field is concerned, has gone full circle, and we are back to politics as usual.

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take steps to end the near-monopoly of major national air routes by Air Canada and permit private airlines to compete on a more equitable basis with Air Canada, and, that permission should be granted to CP Air to extend its transcontinental service to Halifax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to present this motion this afternoon and to discuss for a few moments the three portions of the motion in sequence.
This motion cites the failure by the government opposite to implement a competitive air transportation policy which would recognize the legitimate and rightful aspirations of our private airlines. Indeed, this motion indicts the government for its repeated refusal to pay more than lip service to the common sense principle that private sector airlines be allowed greater freedom to compete with Air Canada.
To be more specific, we in the Progressive Conservative party believe that privately financed airlines should be entitled to a much greater share of the air transportation business in Canada and that future growth mut be directed almost entirely toward these privately-owned enterprises.
At the outset I want to make it clear that the thrust of our argument should in no way be construed as a criticism of Air Canada. In fact in my own riding of Burnaby-Richmond-Del-ta, Air Canada personnel are very active, and I and many of my colleagues on this side of the House enjoy travelling with Air Canada personnel on a weekly basis for many hours. I know the local management of Air Canada in Vancouver, and we on this side of the House are extremely pleased with the senior management of Air Canada as represented by Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
February 23, 1979
Air Transportation
Claude Taylor. Indeed, we could do well with more people like Claude Taylor in this government.
I single out CP Air in the first part of my motion because it is tremendously important to western Canada, but also because it has been identified, as a consequence of transcontinental air policies introduced in the mid-1960s, as the sole second transcontinental air carrier in this country.
CP Air pumps over $280 million annually into the economy of British Columbia and over $1 million of tax revenue into my constituency. It employs over 4,500 people there. By comparison, Air Canada employs 800 people in British Columbia, roughly speaking, and approximately 15,000 in and around the city of Montreal. So if we from the west tend to have some affinity for CP Air, I suppose we have a legitimate reason for it.
The thrust of this motion is not to advocate a reduction of Air Canada's services but rather to ask: should the regional and transcontinental air services in Canada be dominated by one large and centralized national airline? We have only to look at the crippling effects which strikes impose upon our air services to conclude that we should not allow a dominant role to be played by one large nationalized airline in providing air services in this country. The thrust of this motion is that CP Air and regional airlines should enjoy virtually 100 per cent of the future growth at least for the next few years.
I indicated that there were three parts to the motion, and I would like to speak to them in turn. The first section of the motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take steps to end the near-monopoly of major national air routes-
By that I mean the monopoly of transcontinental routes enjoyed by Air Canada. Indeed, I note that recently Mr. Claude Taylor told the press that Air Canada did not enjoy a monopoly. But under the transcontinental policy for the division of services between Air Canada and CP Air as set out in 1977, CP Air was granted only 25 per cent of transcontinental services and Air Canada was granted 75 per cent. If that is not a near-monopoly, I do not know what is.
I should like to read now from a press release put out by the Air Canada information services in September of 1978, a document which surprised me indeed because it sounded more political than factual. In fact there are a few games with numbers here, which surprise because my engineering and scientific background has taught me to trust numbers. But having sat in the House for some weeks and having heard the comments of my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), and having witnessed the introduction of the estimates by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) on Monday evening, I have to believe that numbers do not always tell the truth. There are many games that can be played with numbers, as all hon. members well know. I will read, from this press release issued in September of 1978, a statement relative to CP Air. It is entitled "Air Canada/CP Air Transcontinental Share" and it reads:
[Mr. Siddon.1
-they haven't mounted the full capacity to which they were entitled under government regulations.
In fact they haven't put up their allowable capacity in the past five years.
That is absolutely untrue. CP Air has produced approximately 95 per cent of their allowed capacity in terms of seat-mile service each year since 1975. So any suggestion that they have not put up their allowable capacity is patently untrue. No airline regulated by the Canadian Transport Commission would risk putting up 100 per cent of its capacity because if it put up one extra flight a week, it could well go over the allowed limit and thus contravene their operating licence.
Recently the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has announced an increase to CP Air of some 35 per cent of the growth in transcontinental air traffic for 1978, and 45 per cent of the increase in 1979. That has allowed CP Air to enjoy slightly more of the pie. They now enjoy 27 per cent as opposed to 25 per cent.
I would like to read another portion of the same press release as follows:
Taking only the two companies' major pairs of points, Air Canada currently provides about 60 per cent of the capacity while CP Air provides 40 per cent.
That too is a game with numbers, and it is patently untrue. The next statement reads that if all of Air Canada's services are added, they enjoy 77.5 per cent of the services. So it all depends on how you play with the numbers.
I would like to refer now to the final paragraph of this press release from Air Canada which states:
It should be noted that CP Air picks and chooses the routes it will serve at a frequency giving maximum return.
This is an old chestnut. It is sometimes claimed that Air Canada must serve small traffic centres, while CP Air has been accused of not serving its share of the small traffic generating points in Canada compared with Air Canada. In fact the direct opposite is true. CP Air serves only eight of the top 20 cities in Canada versus Air Canada's 19 of the top 20 cities, and CP Air serves seven of the 45 smaller cities, versus Air Canada's service to only four of them. So of the smallest served, the least frequently served of the 85 airports in Canada, CP Air serves twice as many as does Air Canada. So much for the old chestnut.
Another statement from this presumably correct press release is the following:
For example CP Air provides absolutely no service to Saskatchewan.
Indeed, they do not provide any service to Saskatchewan. They have never been asked to or invited to apply for a licence. In fact at present I understand the volume would not justify it.
I submit that CP Air is the only other transcontinental airline which should be allowed to provide at least 50 per cent of the transcontinental traffic in Canada in the future, and that increase should be gradually phased in over a reasonable period of time.

There is another statistic that might be very interesting to this House. Since 1955 CP Air has transferred 5,700 route miles to regional carriers in Canada, whereas on the other hand Air Canada has transferred only 1,600 route miles. Something is out of whack here, Mr. Speaker. The airline which enjoys prominence in Canada's transcontinental route gives up 1,600 miles, and the airline which enjoys only one-third as much traffic volume gives up more than three times that many route miles. I think something is rather unbalanced, and I believe that statistic to be true.
The second part of my motion states that:

Here 1 am referring to regional policy and third-level air transportation policies which we ought to have in this country. Indeed, in spite of the promises made in this House by the Minister of Transport five years ago, he has yet to set out a policy for third-level air carriers, and the policy relative to regional air service is old and outdated, having been introduced in 1966.
The regional air carriers in Canada are operating in a vacuum. What does the future hold in store for Transair, Pacific Western, Wardair, Great Lakes, Nordair, Quebecair and Eastern Provincial? What does the future hold in store for those airlines? The Minister of Transport is not telling them, and neither is the Canadian Transport Commission.
One thing is certain, and that is the following, the regionals called recently for an immediate review of government policy affecting the future of regional airlines. Something else these regional airlines have suggested is that transcontinental carriers give up some of their route miles to regional carriers on a responsible phase basis.
If you look at the statistics they suggest that CP Air has already given up three times as many route miles as Air Canada. Which should be the first airline to give up some route miles?
I note a headline in a February issue of the Globe and Mail with a picture of Claude Taylor beneath it, which states:
Air Canada president Claude Taylor believes that competition is a two-way street and warns that his airline will be a tough competitor.
That sounds good, but then we start picking up ads in different newspapers. Here is one that says "There's no better choice from Ottawa", and goes on to state:
If your business takes you west, take one of our business machines for the fastest, most frequent service.
Of course that is true because only Air Canada gives you one-stop through service each morning and evening to Vancouver. The ad goes on to state that only Air Canada gives you daily non-stop service to Calgary, and to Edmonton only Air Canada offers daily non-stops. To Winnipeg only Air Canada offers three daily non-stops.
Air Transportation
Let us look at another recent advertisement with a picture of a large fleet of 20 DC9s flying from Ottawa to Toronto. The heading below the picture states "Up to 20 flights a day to and from Toronto". The ad itself goes on to state:
Flights every hour, every week-day, so it's easy to remember the schedule.
I am not attacking Air Canada. I am trying merely to point out here that the Toronto-Ottawa route should properly be viewed as a regional route, as should the Toronto to Montreal route. In fact on the Montreal-Toronto route Air Canada has 30 daily flights, CP has four, and other airlines offer four. On the Toronto-Ottawa flight on the daily "Rapidair" service Air Canada offers 20, once per hour, while other airlines offer four, and CP Air is allowed two. Something is very disproportionate here. This is not a transcontinental airline operation; this is a regional air service and ought rightly to be performed by a private sector airline.
We were all pleased to note that Air Canada is thinking of going private and, indeed, is about to pay or has recently paid its first return to the public purse, amounting to a 4 per cent return on the recent recapitalization of $330 million. I take Mr. Taylor at his word, and I think his record and performance as president of Air Canada have been outstanding, when he suggests the government might want to sell Air Canada. I submit that it should sell Air Canada immediately. It should sell the government's equity through recapitalization, that is, the $330 million used under the restructuring legislation approved by this House in the past year. I suggest that $330 million in capital equity ought to be sold to the private sector in the form of shares to let all Canadians have the chance to own a bigger piece of Air Canada at their discretion rather than by decree.
Finally, the third part of my motion recommends that permission be granted to CP Air to extend its transcontinental service to Halifax. In fact the minister responsible, the Minister of Transport, made a grandiose gesture last November to the effect that he had no objection to allowing the CTC to consider extending CP Air routes east of Montreal. This is very strange coming from the same minister who has delayed repeated requests from CP Air to have its applications received. Be that as it may, the minister has now condescended to receive the application from CP Air, but for the present CP Air is going through the monstrous task of filling out innumerable forms and filing innumerable affidavits in order to prepare itself to appear before the CTC to advance its cause. There again is an example of the problems which our private sector airlines have to contend with when they are dealing with transport regulations in this country-tedious, copious quantities of form filling and red tape.
Referring to the Halifax connection, as I understand it there is absolutely no potential conflict with services into Halifax provided by Eastern Provincial Airways out of Montreal. CP Air is applying for the right to serve Halifax from Toronto only, so it can, indeed, enjoy the title with Air Canada of a transcontinental airline, which means from one side of the continent to the other.

February 23, 1979
Air Transportation
The petitions that CP Air has forwarded to the minister over many recent months have been supported by strong appeals from the chambers of commerce and the city council of Halifax. Indeed, there is no objection and, in fact, there is a strong desire on the part of locals in Halifax that this application be approved. Indeed, the people of Halifax were concerned during a recent Air Canada strike because they lost their service, and it is high time there was an alternative direct connection with Toronto.
In the long-term, CP Air envisages flights to Europe via Halifax. I believe the citizens of Halifax would welcome as long overdue the opportunity to fly to Europe without flying back to Montreal first.
Those are the three elements of my motion. I see I have about one minute left. I would just like to summarize by indicating that on this side of the House we believe that the Canadian Transport Commission has no clearcut regional air transportation policies, and the decisions it makes appear to be based on ad hoc guidelines. There are no specific operating guidelines. The onus seems to be on the applicants to devote tremendous time and cost to the preparation of copious forms and documents to support their applications.
We in the Progressive Conservative party when we form the government will undertake a program of controlled de-regulation. We do not advocate overnight de-regulation along the lines of the recent experiment in the United States, but when one looks to the success of that experiment one has to feel that perhaps there is a lot to be said for allowing much more competition among private sector airlines.
