subsubtopic: SUGGESTION AIR CANADA ROUTES BE GRANTED TO OTHER AIR LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Siddon) who has moved a motion advocating greater competition for Air Canada. It has been moved that the government should take steps to end the near-monopoly of major national air routes by Air Canada; that private airlines should be permitted to compete on a more equitable basis with Air Canada, and, finally, that permission should be granted to CP Air to extend its transcontinental service to Halifax. I want to say, immediately, Mr. Speaker, that I consider the steps the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta has proposed the government take have merit. Indeed, they have such considerable merit that the government has already taken the very actions proposed by him.
As long ago as 1976, it was recognized that certain changes of the kind proposed in the first part of the member's motion could and should be made with respect to Air Canada's role. That is why the government prepared new legislation concerning Air Canada. On October 28, 1976 a new "act respecting the reorganization of Air Canada" was given first reading in this House. The Air Canada Act, 1977, was subsequently assented to on February 2, 1978. That legislation served, among other things, to put Air Canada on the same basis as other carriers in obtaining licence authority for new routes
[Mr. Siddon. 1
before the Canadian Transport Commission. Or, as the hon. member has expressed it, this act permitted private airlines to compete on a more equitable basis with Air Canada. I will explain this in some detail later.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I would like to challenge the allegation that Air Canada has a "near-monopoly of major national air routes". I believe that the facts suggest otherwise and I will present some in a few moments to show why. Finally, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member moved that permission be granted to CP Air to extend its transcontinental services to Halifax. In fact, on November 7, 1978, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) announced that the government has no objection to CP Air applying to the Canadian Transport Commission to operate into the Atlantic provinces, in conformity with the CTC's regulatory requirements.
I would like to examine the three parts of this motion in some detail, Mr. Speaker. I will begin with the first part of it: that the government should take steps to end the near-monopoly of major national air routes by Air Canada. I suggest that this part of the motion is more an allegation than a proposed action. It is an allegation that Air Canada does, in fact, have "a near-monopoly on major national air routes". I suggest that we should examine this allegation closely.
What is a "near-monopoly"? A monopoly is, literally, exclusive possession or control. So I suppose that a "near-monopoly" is exclusive possession or control of most, but not quite all, the major national air routes.
Next, we must try to determine what a "major national air route" is. There is no single accepted definition of a major national air route and I do not know what definition the hon. member may have in mind. I would therefore like to suggest three different ways in which "a major national air route" might be defined and to discuss these with reference to Air Canada's alleged monopoly of them.
One definition of a national air route-perhaps almost too facile a definition-is a route which stretches across the entire country, a route from sea to sea that links major cities on the east coast with major centres on the west coast. Let us look at a few examples of such routes to see just what kind of a monopoly Air Canada has. First, St. John's to Victoria: no carrier, of course, offers a direct flight between these two cities. It is necessary to make connections. Air Canada, as the national carrier, naturally provides a service between these two provincial capitals, connecting in Montreal or Toronto. But it is also possible to fly on Eastern Provincial Airways to Montreal-though, granted, not on a direct flight-and the rest of the way on CP Air. The same possibilities exist between Halifax and Vancouver.
Certain other east to west coast linkages are not, in fact, totally served by Air Canada. From, say, Charlottetown or Moncton to Prince Rupert or Kamloops, it is necessary to
February 23, 1979

travel on carriers other than Air Canada part of the way. This is because Air Canada is not intended to serve all centres. Under Canadian air transportation policy, other carriers are intended to serve such centres. This means that Air Canada cannot possibly have a near-monopoly on all east to west coast routes. More will be said about the roles of Air Canada and the other carriers later.
A second way of defining "major national air routes" would be to look at those city pairs which generated the greatest numbers of passengers travelling between them. In 1977, the latest year for which complete figures are available, the following city-pairs, in the order of their ranking, experienced the highest traffic volumes: Montreal-Toronto, Ottawa-Toronto, Calgary-Edmonton, Toronto-Vancouver, Calgary-Vancouver, Edmonton-Vancouver, Toronto-Winnipeg, Calgary-Toronto, Halifax-Toronto and Edmonton-Toronto.
1 would like to examine each of these high traffic routes to see whether they are served by other scheduled air carriers or whether Air Canada has a monopolistic grip on the most highly travelled routes. First, Montreal-Toronto: this route is served by CP Air, Air Canada and Nordair. Second, Ottawa-Toronto: served by CP Air, Air Canada, Nordair, Great Lakes Airlines and Otonabee Airways. Third, Calgary-Edmonton: served only by PWA. Fourth, Toronto-Vancouver: served by CP Air and Air Canada directly and by Transair and PWA on an indirect service. Fifth, Calgary-Vancouver: served by CP Air, Air Canada and PWA. Sixth, Edmonton-Vancouver: similarly served by CP Air, Air Canada and PWA. Seventh, Toronto-Winnipeg: served by Air Canada and Nordair. Eighth, Calgary-Toronto: served directly by CP Air and Air Canada, and by Transair and Nordair on an indirect service.
Ninth, Halifax-Toronto: served by Air Canada at present, but both CP Air and EPA have expressed interest in serving this route. And, as I mentioned earlier, the Minister of Transport has specifically announced that the government would have no objection to CP Air applying to the Canadian Transport Commission to operate into the Atlantic provinces.
Tenth, Edmonton-Toronto: like Calgary-Toronto, served directly by CP Air and Air Canada, and by Transair and Nordair on an indirect service.
Mr. Speaker, I have just described the scheduled air services available on the ten most travelled air routes in the country. On nine of those routes Air Canada has at least one competitor. On the tenth, Toronto-Halifax, there is a good possibility that Air Canada will soon have competition. I ask: is this evidence that Air Canada has a near-monopolistic grip on major routes in this country?
If some members of this House remain unconvinced that Air Canada does not have competition on "major national air routes", let me cite a third way of defining such routes. This definition is in terms of route length. Those routes which it is
Air Transportation
most appropriate that the national carriers-Air Canada and CP Air-serve are obviously the long-haul and medium-haul routes, say, all those over 500 miles, as measured by great circle mileages. Although I might mention, parenthetically, that under Canadian air transportation policy, the regional air carriers have been given authority for certain long-haul routes, notably in the north.
I would like to cite a random selection of medium and long-haul routes, excluding those I have already mentioned, and to indicate, as I just did for the most travelled routes, which carriers serve these routes.
First, Gander-Halifax; 506 great circle miles: served by Air Canada and EPA.
Second, Montreal-Windsor; 509 great circle miles: served by Air Canada and Nordair.
Third, Edmonton-Winnipeg; 738 great circle miles: served by Air Canada and Transair.
Fourth, Wabush-Montreal; 600 great circle miles: served by Quebecair.
Fifth, Yellowknife-Edmonton; 633 great circle miles: served by PWA.
I could continue with examples, Mr. Speaker, but I believe the point is made once again. On what might logically be defined as "major national air routes", Air Canada simply does not have a monopoly-or a near-monopoly. It has competition.
Mr. Speaker, having pointed out that Air Canada does have competition on major national air routes, I would like to provide some background concerning Air Canada and its evolving role and the evolving nature of the air transportation industry in general. I believe that this background may provide some explanation as to why the hon. member felt that Air Canada has a near-monopoly position on major air routes. Certainly this was the case at one time but, as I am going to explain, there were valid reasons for this situation.
Air Canada was, of course, originally known as Trans-Canada Airlines and incorporated under the Trans-Canada Airlines Act, passed in 1937. Trans-Canada Airlines was established as a Crown corporation specifically to serve as the national air carrier-a leader, a pioneer and developer in making air services available across the country. TCA was also to provide efficient services without a government subsidy.
The history of TCA-which became Air Canada in 1965- has been one of almost continuous growth. In 1939, TCA linked Vancouver and Montreal for the first time with a scheduled passenger air service, using small Lockheeds. The next year, it extended its budding transcontinental services to Moncton. In 1941, it achieved sea to sea service with the start of flights to Halifax. After the war, TCA continued its development of domestic services as well as transborder and international services. In the 1950s, it had acquired the Super
3562

February 23, 1979

Constellation, seating 75 passengers and in 1955 became the first North American airline to introduce the comfort and speed of propeller turbine aircraft when the first of 51 British-built Vickers Viscounts was introduced on Canadian routes. In 1960, Air Canada introduced the commercial jet age to Canada when it started using the DC-8 from Vancouver to Montreal.
During the 1960s, Air Canada retired many of its early piston-engine aircraft and became the first airline in North America with an all-turbine fleet. In 1971, Air Canada introduced the first wide-body jet on its routes, the Boeing 747.
I have mentioned these vignettes of Air Canada's history in order to convey a sense of how it has changed in the forty years since it was established. At the same time, the entire Canadian air transportation industry has evolved as well.
After a study in the late 1950s by a British transport expert, Mr. Stephen Wheatcroft, competition was allowed on certain routes. But in a policy statement in 1964, the then Minister of Transport, Mr. Pickersgill, stated that:
In the domestic mainline field, while the principle of competition is not rejected, any development of competition should not compromise or seriously injure the economic viability of IC As main line domestic operations which represent the essential framework of its network of domestic services. In other words, there must not be the kind of competition which would put TCA into the red; and, in the event that competition continues, the air transport board should ensure an opportunity for growth to both lines above this basic minimum.
These words may sound unnecessarily cautious, but I think that we should remember that, if one airline can handle the available business-as Air Canada was generally doing-and another carrier is introduced in order to provide competition, it follows that the profits of the original carrier will decline. Indeed, profits would decline sufficiently to "put TCA into the red", as Mr. Pickersgill mentioned.
The mid-1960s were a time of substantial change in the Canadian air carrier industry. During this period, the regional air carriers started to become an increasingly important force within the aviation industry. In 1966, this role was clarified in a policy statement by the Ministei of Transport, who stated that:
The role of regional carriers is to operate regional routes to supplement the domestic mainline operations of Air Canada and CPA and to provide regular and scheduled service into the north. They will not become directly competitive on any substantial scale with the two mainline carriers. Routes which because of volume of traffic, size of airports and related facilities, or suitable type of aircraft, do not fit the type of mainline operations of Air Canada or CPA will be reserved for regional carriers or, in some cases, may be transferred to them. The principal deciding factor should be the nature of the route. The Air Transport Board will be responsible for determining what routes are suitable for the regional carriers. Regional carriers will be expected to operate on a regional basis and will not be authorized to expand as potential transcontinental carriers. While rigid definition of boundaries for any one regional carrier is neither practical nor desirable, the main operations of each carrier will be carried on in one region.
Economic and efficient operation of a regional route pattern may in some cases involve competition with Air Canada or CPA on a mainline route segment. In such cases, the regional carriers can be authorized to be operated in competition with Air Canada or CPA.
{Mr. Savard.l
I would now like to refer to the second part of the hon. member's motion, in which he asked that private airlines be permitted to compete on a more equitable basis with Air Canada. It is correct that, at one time, other carriers were not on quite the same footing as Air Canada. This is because Air Canada's behaviour was governed by the Air Canada contract with the federal government. By virtue of this contract, pursuant to section 14 of the Air Canada Act, Air Canada provided domestic service outside the Canadian Transport Commission normal regulatory powers.

Let me say it comes as no surprise to me when a member of the Progressive Conservative party wants to expand the role of private enterprise in our airlines system, and in so doing to cut down on the role of the publicly owned line known as Air Canada. That is in keeping with the philosophy of that party, and it is to be expected that that point of view would be presented by them in this House.
As a matter of fact it was when the present member for Prince Edward-Hasting (Mr. Hees) was the minister of transport that, for the first time, a line other than Trans-Canada Airlines, as it was known then, was given rights on the transcontinental route. So the proposal being put forward today is simply an extension of Conservative philosophy. However, I must say that I feel quite disturbed and unhappy when I hear a spokesman from the Liberal side of the House say that there is merit in this motion and that there is much in it that the government is already doing.
I am even more disturbed when I read in newspapers and when I hear the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Siddon) quote a statement made by Mr. Claude Taylor,

Members are used to my getting into debates and reciting ancient history, but it is usually in my favourite field of pensions that I do this. But there was some other ancient history going through my mind this afternoon. My friend from across the way referred to the organization of Trans-Canada Airlines in 1937-that was before I was here in this House- but in the middle 1940s we had quite serious discussions about post-war civil aviation policy. We had a policy laid down by the then prime minister, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, and we had some interesting contributions made by the minister who was in charge, namely, the Right Hon. Clarence Decatur Howe.
I remember very well-I am trying to think what year it was but I cannot recall if it was just before the end of the war or just after it, but it was certainly in the middle forties-Mr. Howe standing up and telling us he had tried his best to get the Canadian Pacific Railway to come in with the Canadian National Railways on the organization of Trans-Canada Airlines. But, said Mr. Howe, Canadian Pacific was not interested. Why? Because there was no money to be made in the operation at that time. That is what drove C. D. Howe to a form of public ownership, namely, establishing Trans-Canada Airlines under full public ownership.

speechtext:
-I rise with some trepidation when I follow such a distinguished veteran member of the House of Commons as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). But I have to say that I will look in Hansard at the first paragraph in his intervention in this debate because it expresses precisely what the Progressive Conservative party stands for and precisely our opposition to this stand that our frieds to the left take in this case.
However, I rise to support in principle the spirit of this motion by my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond-Delta (Mr. Siddon) specifically, and very briefly, because it is rather late on Friday afternoon, but I want to deal with that section of his motion which reads:
Permit private airlines to compete on a more equitable basis with Air Canada.
Hon. members will know, since I am sure that all my [DOT] colleagues read all speeches made in Hansard as diligently as I

February 23, 1979
Air Transportation
do, that I have voiced concern in this Elouse about Air Canada taking over Nordair, a highly successful privately-owned regional airline and one which provides an essential service to southern Ontario and to my own area of Hamilton. Indeed, it has now been extended to the city of Winnipeg, the home of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Hon. members will also recall the high and heavy flak which the government received from many sources, such as the airline industry, the private sector, employees of Nordair, and especially the media whose editorials roundly condemned the idea of a big government airline which has enough of its own troubles, diluting the effectiveness and crippling the entrepreneurial efficiency of a privately-owned regional operation like Nordair. There were even fears in my area that Hamilton's service would not only deteriorate with Air Canada's absorption of Nordair, but that the government-owned airline might one day need to consolidate its operations and we could lose the kind of valuable service that Nordair provides to our area, altogether. I have since had those fears put to rest by persons I trust who are knowledgeable in the field. As the industrial capital of Canada, Hamilton and its civic airport will continue to enjoy some ongoing and perhaps expanded regional air service to serve southwestern Ontario, northern New York State, and perhaps a direct Hamilton-Winnipeg route.
The question that still remains, and it is very germane to this debate, is what is Nordair's future now that Air Canada has been given a mandate by the government to reprivatize the regional carrier within the space of a year from last October. What will the eventual role of Air Canada be as the government agent in this sale? How will Nordair, and in the larger context Air Canada, fit into the government's over-all rationalization of the several regional carriers in central and eastern Canada?
With this government's recent stampede to the right, and its determination suddenly to honour the private sector of this country's economy, I cannot believe that it will not use every chance to continue its inevitable encroachment on free enterprise in Canada. The thinking of this administration has always been that the government can do better. What the Liberals and our friends to the left do not tell us is the corollary of this, that it is the extended version of Murphy's law. If something can go wrong, it will, only the Canadian taxpayer has to foot the bill. I am not saying that any government involvement is wrong. In the case of Air Canada's participation and Ottawa's over-all plan for rationalizing the airlines, a limited role is desirable.
For many years I have been a supporter of Air Canada in the national role that this parliament has given it to perform. It does not always do that well. Until recently, labour-management relations have been lousy.
I approve of some Air Canada participation in our national airline transportation system. For example, some of the applicants who want to buy Nordair, such as Great Lakes, Quebe-

cair, plus other regional airlines in eastern Canada such as Eastern Provincial Airways and Nordair itself-all have their reservations systems run by Air Canada. My information is that almost without exception every applicant for Nordair has stipulated that they want Air Canada's participation to the extent of 10 per cent to 15 per cent to 20 per cent. Therefore, there is a desire to see Air Canada maintain a role in regional and third carrier operations for the sake of continuity, experience and, to a certain extent, security. However, I emphasize that whatever emerges from the hot and heavy negotiations now going on in Montreal, I would be concerned about the over-all Air Canada involvement in a regional air service.
Like my colleague from Burnaby-Richmond-Delta I too take Air Canada president Claude Taylor as a straightforward, objective, and tough negotiator. The problem I am told that Mr. Taylor faces, and something that should concern our party and indeed the Canadian people, is this. None of these applicants really have enough money to put together a whole regional airline which stretches from Newfoundland to Winnipeg. The capital base for such a carrier with common equipment, 737 aircraft, could be in excess of $100 million. However, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) still thinks there should be a great megalopolis of a regional carrier which stretches from Newfoundland to the Great Lakes and beyond. On the other hand, people I have talked to feel there is a definite autonomous desire on the part of Ontario interests, Quebec interests and Atlantic Canada.
In conclusion, I intend to ask the Minister of Transport at the earliest opportunity, on Monday if he is back in the House, whether he will allow his rationalization of regional airlines to proceed along a regional and geographical basis, that is, autonomously owned and operated regional services in Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada, or whether the minister is determined to go with one single regional carrier with the commonality of equipment from St. John's to Winnipeg. I will also be asking the minister about the widely rumoured merger of Quebecair and Nordair, to be headquartered in Montreal.
There is one other fear that has been expressed to me and which I voice to the House at this late hour. Given this government's financial and labour management record with many of its Crown corporations, there is a fear on the part of many people that if Air Canada cannot find a satisfactory buyer, the Government of Canada might resort to setting up yet another Crown corporation to oversee all the regional airlines in eastern and central Canada. That would be tragic.
In short, we on this side look forward to hearing before this parliament comes to an end the transport minister's long promised and eagerly awaited policy on just how much scope the government will allow private regional operations in eastern and central Canada to carry on, and just how much competition Nordair, Quebecair, Great Lakes and Eastern Provincial Airways from whatever emerges out of this rationalization policy will be allowed with the very firmly established government-owned airline, Air Canada.

take part in this debate. I do not know how often I have stood on the floor of this House over the past six years to defend Air Canada against those who would nationalize, privatize it, or just disband it. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) need not worry that we are going to let Air Canada disappear as the Tories would have happen.
We never hear from those on the other side that the province of Alberta had no business nationalizing an airline, that it had no business buying enough pieces to put together the better part of a national airline. That kind of socialization and nationalization is fine.
When PWA bought out Transair, which serviced Thunder Bay, because of the idea of only having two national carriers, this almost forced Nordair into government hands. The Tories must decide whether theirs is a party for the good of this country or just to deal with and support provincial aims.
